newsitem.title: USA: No blue moon, but blue sunsets on red planet?.
newsitem.headline: No blue moon, but blue sunsets on red planet?.

text.p: With a U.S. spacecraft less than a million miles from an American Independence Day landing on Mars, scientists speculated on Wednesday that sunsets on the "red planet" might appear blue.

At a briefing just two days before the Pathfinder is scheduled to crash-land on Earth's closest planetary neighbour, the scientists could barely contain their excitement at what they might learn about Mars.

After the Pathfinder -- three unfolding steel and graphite units -- sets foot on the planet's surface on Friday, a dune-buggy type vehicle called the "Mars Rover" will roll down a ramp to begin a one-week survey, charting the composition and size of Martian rocks, dust and debris.
Peter Smith, who heads the Pathfinder's imaging team, said the sophisticated two-lens camera on the Rover will zoom in on the Martian landscape.
But if it looked to the horizon, he told reporters, it might see a blue sunset.
"Think about an Earth sunset," he said. "The gas layer scatters the blue light and what we see is red."
"Well, dust on Mars is red, so it's probable red light will scatter and you will see a blueish disk," said Smith of the University of Arizona.

If humans ever visit Mars, however, they would have to combat frigid temperatures before watching the blue sun go down. Temperatures on the planet ranged from a mild minus 10 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 23 C) to minus 127 (minus 88 C), which is the coldest temperature ever recorded on Earth.

The landing and the subsequent exploration of a tiny portion of the planet's surface by the Rover will eventually lead to a human expedition to Mars, according to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration.
At NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, scientists were optimistic about their latest venture to Mars -- the last was 21 years ago with the Viking orbiter and lander.
JPL scientist John Schofield said the Pathfinder was hurtling towards Mars on Wednesday at about 4 miles (6.5 km) per second, meaning it was some 800,000 miles (1,280,000 km) from impact.
The first images, expected to be beamed back on Friday afternoon, take about 10 minutes to travel the 119 million miles (191 million km) to Earth.
One of the questions the scientists in Pasadena and their colleagues around the world hoped to answer was whether there could have been life on the planet, which is about half the size of Earth.
But on Wednesday they warned against such expectations.
Geologist Rudolf Rieder, of Germany's Max Planck Institute in Mainz, cautioned: "We will not be able to determine traces of life."

But the equipment on the Rover will be able to analyse rock and soil samples and answer questions such as whether meteorites actually came from Mars, and what processes transformed rock into soil, he said.
And JPL's William Folkner, who is in charge of studying Mars' rotational orbit and radio signals from the planet, said: "Don't expect any trace of life unless we get some unusual radio signals."

Meanwhile, the scientists in charge of the Pathfinder Mission admit that Friday will be a nail-biting, anxiety-ridden day as they wait to learn if 3 1/2 years of hard work, experimentation and fly-by-the-seat-of-your-pants innovation will work.
Their greatest concern was that after a journey of 309 million miles (497 million km) Pathfinder, launched on Dec. 4, 1996, will land in unknown terrain and in unknown atmospheric conditions.

The three-part spacecraft, made up of the cruise module which took the craft on its seven-month journey to Mars, the landing craft, and the Rover and its attendant base, have performed "flawlessly," according to Brian Muirhead, the assistant project manager and head of flight systems.
But there are several unknowns: It will be the first time that a spacecraft has landed on another planet without first orbiting it.
